Article Title: 8 months, Moscow-to-Munich flights, but now he is 'fed up': Behind Russia No. 1 Ian Nepomniachtchi's tattoos
Article Text:
Ian Nepomniachtchi and his tattoos (Photos by Jyotirmoy Halder from TimesofIndia.com)

Ian Nepomniachtchi's tattoo on his right arm (Photos by Jyotirmoy Halder from TimesofIndia.com)

A test of patience off the board

Ian Nepomniachtchi's tattoo on his left arm (Photos by Jyotirmoy Halder from TimesofIndia.com)

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

BENGALURU: The word “tattoo” is believed to have come from Polynesian languages, particularly words such as "tatau", a term associated with traditional body art in that region. European sailors encountered Polynesian tattooing and helped carry the word back into European languages. Even thousands of years earlier, ancient Egyptians were already tattooing their bodies, with some of the earliest known examples found on female mummies. Researchers suggest that their markings may have served social, ritual or protective purposes.Millennia later, tattoos still carry stories. On the arms of Russia’s top-ranked chess grandmaster Ian Nepomniachtchi, they surely do.A two-time back-to-back winner of the prestigious Candidates Tournament, Nepomniachtchi, affectionately known in the chess world simply as "Nepo", was initially slated to fly from Moscow to Bengaluru on September 2 for the Global Chess League (GCL).Opting to delay his travel, he touched down on the morning of September 4, a day before the start of the tournament. The late arrival has effectively cost him any chance for local sightseeing, but the city has still managed to win him over."I really like the climate; it's very mild compared to what I'm used to in India when I visited previously. And yeah, the place is very nice," Nepo told TimesofIndia.com with a smile during an exclusive interaction as his team, Ganges Grandmasters, opened their GCL campaign with a victory on Saturday.Whether you were inside the arena or watching from a screen, Nepomniachtchi’s arms were hard to miss. At a glance, they looked less like a grandmaster’s limbs and more like a vivid canvas, covered in colours and intricate artwork that stood out against the otherwise restrained setting of professional chess.The elite circuit is a world of pristine blazers, pressed shirts and strict sartorial codes, where body art is rarely part of the picture. Here, at GCL, that is not the case."Normally, it's not approved by the dress code. So, this is only for a gym," Nepo admitted, laughing as he rolled back his sleeves to reveal his tattoo.When asked how many he has. "Not that much, only two," he replied. On his right arm carries a powerful mantra. “Rise and rise again and again like the Phoenix from the ashes; until the lambs have become lions.”"I have this one, but this comes from 2023. I think I played the first GCL right after getting this," he explained. "I like this quote. This I wanted to get many, many years before. It's always hard to make a decision to get something onto your skin."The process for his right arm was surprisingly painless, which gave the grandmaster a false sense of security."This one felt so easy," Nepo recalled. "So, I felt, alright, maybe the full-sleeve is fine. Why not?"That casual "why not" evolved into an agonising, transatlantic project on his left arm that would test his endurance on another level."My nickname is Lachesis, and it's the Greek goddess of fate," he told this website, referencing his popular social media handle, lachesisq. "I wanted a Greek goddess, and it took me some time to find a master, an artist who specialises (in this)."Nepo eventually found the right artist, but that artist was in Germany."The artist I was working with is based in Munich," he revealed. "It was logistically a bit tricky as I live in Moscow. We completed several sessions, and eventually, it was eight sessions total starting from September and ending in April."The resulting full-sleeve is what one can call a chef-d'œuvre. "Eventually, it's a mix of ideas," the Russian grandmaster stated while examining the ink. "You have some snake for Ouroboros and also some chess pieces for whatever reason, but it was an idea from my artist, and I didn't really argue."But for the 36-year-old Nepo, it was a classic case of no pain, no gain."This one (right arm) was completely painless, and this (left arm) was a hell of a time," he confessed. "I finished it (the left one) this year, but it's a full sleeve. It was quite painful, to be honest, and it took a while.So, for now, I'm fed up with pain. I was patient; I tolerated a lot."Read Also: 'Gukesh's lifetime dream just came too early': American GM Levon Aronian assesses Sindarov clash | Exclusive Now that the suffering has ended with its completion, he doesn't plan on returning to the tattoo chair anytime soon. Now, he just hopes that people can see, and understand, the meaning behind the artwork."And this is supposed to be a phoenix," he said with a final grin, gesturing to his right arm, "if it's recognisable or not."
Article Summary: Russian chess grandmaster Ian Nepomniachtchi has two tattoos. The 36-year-old was in Bengaluru for the Global Chess League (GCL) He is a two-time back-to-back winner of the prestigious Candidates Tournament. The process for his right arm was surprisingly painless.

Article Title: 'Really like his chess, not his personality': Russia No. 1 Nepo on Hans Niemann's 'FIDE must punish' remarks | Exclusive
Article Text:
Ian Nepomniachtchi and Hans Niemann

What triggered the reaction from Hans

Nepo on Hans Niemann's " Untold: Chess Mates " documentary

BENGALURU: Ian Nepomniachtchi, also known as "Nepo", has little doubt about Hans Niemann’s ability on the chessboard. Away from it, however, the Russian grandmaster remains less impressed.Reacting to Niemann’s recent call for FIDE to punish players who make public accusations or insinuations, particularly involving young players, Nepomniachtchi said the American grandmaster “can’t stop playing the victim card”.“First of all, Hans can’t stop playing the victim card. He pretty much lives in that skin. I think there was a fair reason, from his online performances through many years, as far as I know, to be cautious about Hans himself,” Nepo, Russia’s No. 1 player, told TimesofIndia.com in an exclusive interaction on the sidelines of the Global Chess League (GCL).Despite the friction, Nepomniachtchi feels that Niemann has established himself as a strong player. “As for Hans right now, he proves himself as a very good and formidable player. I really like the way he plays chess, though I don’t like his personality. As a chess player, he plays quite well, and in certain openings, he’s quite good at,” he added.At the same time, Nepo also believes Niemann is quick to seize opportunities to provoke a reaction. “Whenever he has an opportunity to bite anyone and seek for some reaction, he immediately does this. Maybe for him, it’s fine for his overall image,” he said.Drawing a comparison with mixed martial arts star Conor McGregor, he said Niemann appears to have embraced a similarly controversial image in chess.“Conor McGregor has 'The Notorious' nickname in MMA. Hans surely tries to be some notorious chess player. So that’s what he does,” Nepomniachtchi said.The comments come after Niemann criticised Nepomniachtchi over remarks made during an online game against 14-year-old Canadian chess player Aaron Mendes.Mendes defeated Nepomniachtchi in Round 10 of the Titled Tuesday event on September 1. During his stream, Nepomniachtchi questioned Mendes’ decision to play an en passant capture instead of giving check.“I would have zero suspicions about this game, but his en passant instead of a check, it leaves a bad taste. Why? How? For what? Aaron, my friend… Fortunately, we will not play against Aaron again in the tournament, because we already learned our lesson from him,” Nepomniachtchi had said.Niemann subsequently called on FIDE to take action against players who make public accusations or insinuations, particularly when young players are involved.“FIDE must punish players for public accusations and insinuations, especially regarding a 14-year-old,” Niemann wrote on X, adding that genuine concerns should instead be taken to FIDE’s Ethics Commission.Asked about the Netflix documentary "Untold: Chess Mates", which revisits the cheating controversy surrounding Niemann, Nepomniachtchi said it did not reveal much that was new to him.“I was sort of inside of this. I was playing the same tournament. I didn’t find out anything new. Some of it was more or less obvious,” he revealed.“Everything was on the surface. But the most disappointing thing in the documentary is that there is no answer. I expected it as a usual chess fan.”For those looking to get introduced to chess, however, Nepomniachtchi had another recommendation. “If you want to get introduced to chess, I would better suggest you watch "The Queen of Chess" about Judit Polgar. That was an awesome one.”
Article Summary: Hans Niemann criticised Ian Nepomniachtchi over remarks made during an online game against 14-year-old Canadian chess player Aaron Mendes. “I really like the way he plays chess, though I don’t like his personality. As a chess player, he plays quite well, and in certain openings, he’s quite good at,” he said.

Article Title: Eight runs from one ball: Andrew Symonds produced one of Test cricket’s strangest feats, but it still wasn’t the highest ever
Article Text:
Andrew Symonds’ eight-run madness at the Gabba

How Symonds ran eight off one ball

Symonds was not the only batter to score eight

Brian Lara

Nine runs from one ball is even rarer

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Andrew Symonds once produced one of the rarest scoring feats in Test cricket, collecting eight runs from a single delivery during Australia's Test against New Zealand at the Gabba in Brisbane in 2008-09.The bizarre sequence involved an all-run four followed by four overthrows, with New Zealand fast bowler Iain O'Brien at the centre of the drama. There was an added twist to the incident, as O'Brien had seen Symonds dropped off the previous delivery before eventually dismissing him just two balls later.Australia were 124 for four in the 46th over after Ricky Ponting had decided to bat in Brisbane.O'Brien opened the over with a bouncer, which Symonds ducked under. The bowler went short again with his next delivery, and this time Symonds pulled the ball towards mid-wicket.However, Aaron Redmond put down the chance.O'Brien responded as fast bowlers often do after a missed opportunity, sending down another short delivery. This time, the ball was outside off-stump and Symonds attacked it ferociously with a pull.The enormous Gabba outfield slowed the ball down, but Symonds and Michael Clarke had already completed three runs by the time Redmond got to it.The pair then decided to push for another run, hoping to take advantage of the throw.That decision produced chaos.New Zealand wicketkeeper Brendon McCullum moved across to collect the return. He gathered the ball, turned and threw it towards the stumps, only to discover that Symonds had already made his ground.There was another problem for New Zealand. Nobody was positioned behind the wicketkeeper to stop the throw.The ball therefore continued all the way to the boundary. Symonds had effectively turned a pull shot into an extraordinary eight-run haul.Umpire Rudi Koertzen then signalled the total by raising eight fingers, meaning eight runs were added to Australia's score and Symonds' tally.It was two more than the figure commonly described as the maximum possible from a single delivery and even one more than the total India received in a penalty-run incident against Bangladesh at Chattogram.Symonds' eight-run delivery was only the fourth known instance of eight runs being scored from a single ball in Test cricket at that point.The first recorded example came in Melbourne during the 1928-29 series, which was also the final Test of Don Bradman's first series.England's Patsy Hendren scored eight after completing four runs and then benefiting from four overthrows off Australian debutant Percy Hornibrook.Another unusual eight-run delivery occurred in Melbourne during the 1980-81 season.New Zealand's John Wright was the beneficiary on that occasion. He ran four before four overthrows followed after Rod Marsh collected the fielder's return and threw the ball towards the stumps. The throw escaped and Wright picked up the additional runs off Lenny Pascoe's delivery.The other known instance before Symonds came in Port-of-Spain during the 2004-05 season. Brian Lara glanced a delivery from South Africa's slow left-armer Nicky Boje for three. South African wicketkeeper Mark Boucher chased the ball and threw it back towards the field.However, Boucher's return struck a fielder's helmet that had been left on the ground.That resulted in five penalty runs being awarded, taking Lara's total from the delivery to eight.Under the rules at the time, those five runs would previously have been credited to Lara. Following a recent rule change, they were instead recorded as penalty extras.Lara, who was on his way to a huge score, would eventually be dismissed for 196.Eight runs from one delivery are extraordinarily unusual, but first-class cricket has witnessed an even greater number.There have been 14 recorded instances of a batter running nine runs from a single ball in first-class cricket. Remarkably, none of those instances came after 1949.Only one of those 14 was achieved without the help of overthrows. Frederick Ponsonby of the MCC managed it against Cambridge University at Parker's Piece in Cambridge in 1842.Even that record was surpassed in unusual circumstances by Samuel Wood of Derbyshire against Cuthbert Burnup of the MCC at Lord's in 1900.That match was played during an experimental period involving the 'revised net system'. Boundaries were removed at some first-class matches and replaced by high nets surrounding the playing area.With no boundaries to end a run, batters had to keep running for every scoring opportunity.It was a completely different approach to scoring, but it also produced one of cricket's most extraordinary statistical records.Symonds' eight at the Gabba, meanwhile, remains one of the game's most memorable examples of how a single delivery can turn into complete chaos, combining a powerful shot, aggressive running and a disastrous throw into one remarkable sequence.
Article Summary: Andrew Symonds scored eight runs from a single delivery during Australia's Test against New Zealand at the Gabba in Brisbane in 2008-09. The bizarre sequence involved an all-run four followed by four overthrows, with New Zealand fast bowler Iain O'Brien at the centre of the drama. There have been 14 recorded instances of a batter running nine runs in a single ball in first-class cricket.

Article Title: Seven wickets in 21 balls: Sri Lanka's Chamari Athapaththu scripts history with record-breaking spell
Article Text:
Chamari Athapaththu

Defending champions Sri Lanka moved to the top of Group B in the Women's Asia Cup after beating Indonesia by 75 runs in Dubai on Thursday, thanks to captain Chamari Athapaththu's record seven-wicket haul and Nilakshika Silva's half-century.Sri Lanka were defending a modest target of 125 on a slow-paced pitch, but Athapaththu turned the match around with one of the best bowling performances in women's T20 internationals.She came on to bowl in the fourth over and struck with her fourth, seventh and eighth deliveries. Although she missed out on a hat-trick in that over, she completed it later by taking three wickets in three balls across two overs.Athapaththu finished with 7/5 in 21 balls, becoming the first bowler from a Full Member nation to take seven wickets in a women's T20I. The previous best figures in women's T20Is belonged to Zimbabwe's Esther Mbofana, who took 6/11 against Eswatini in 2021.Indonesia were bowled out for 49. Rahmawati Pangestuti scored 10, while Ni Made Putri Suwandewi remained unbeaten on 12. No other Indonesian batter reached double figures.Earlier, Sri Lanka were in trouble at 62/6 before Nilakshika Silva scored 50 off 35 balls to lift them to 124/7.For Indonesia, Ni Luh Dewi was the pick of the bowlers with 3/32.The win took Sri Lanka to the top of Group B in the Women's Asia Cup.In Group A, India remain on top of the standings, with Pakistan in second place.Meanwhile, India's vice-captain Smriti Mandhana also made history during India's Group A match against Hong Kong in Dubai. The 30-year-old went past Mithali Raj to become the highest run-scorer in women's international cricket across all formats.
Article Summary: Sri Lanka beat Indonesia by 75 runs in the Women's Asia Cup in Dubai. Captain Chamari Athapaththu took a record seven-wicket haul. Nilakshika Silva scored 50 off 35 balls to lift Sri Lanka to 124/7.

Article Title: ‘AAF risk’: Herbal supplements put India’s Asian Games athletes under scanner
Article Text:
Herbal Supplemets (Representational Image)

Unprecedented scrutiny

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Bengaluru: With Athletics Integrity Unit (AIU) officials conducting random checks on India’s elite athletes preparing for the Asian Games, experts are concerned that the use of herbal supplements by top athletes could result in Adverse Analytical Findings (AAF) when samples are tested for performance-enhancing substances at WADA-accredited laboratories abroad.According to experts, the use of herbal supplements is quite common among athletes training in national camps.“Among the supplements commonly used by our athletes are kida jadi buti, bhasmas, ashwagandha and shilajit. Kida jadi (Cordyceps sinensis) is the most expensive of the lot, retailing at Rs 16-20 lakh per kilogram. It is consumed after being mixed with honey,” they told TOI.In India, kida jadi is listed on e-commerce platforms at around Rs 1.66 lakh for 100g.“There are many athletes who use their savings to buy kida jadi and consume it regularly. There is a risk of an AAF for athletes using herbal supplements, as many of these products are not tested for their ingredients. For a month’s course, they may have to shell out around Rs 1 lakh.“A lot of our sprinters, throwers and middle-distance runners are taking these supplements,” they said, adding that most athletes do not disclose their use of herbal supplements when declaring the list of supplements they consume.Kida jadi is a type of fungus sourced from the Himalayas. Indian athletes have been using it for many years and none have returned a positive result so far. However, there have recently been concerns that some products may contain substances on WADA’s banned list, though nothing has been confirmed yet.“These metabolites may not have triggered a positive result in NADA tests, but in advanced tests conducted by the AIU, the outcome could be different, putting our athletes at risk of an AAF,” experts said.Asked about the use of locally sourced herbal supplements, Mihira Khopkar, who served as the Indian contingent’s nutritionist at the Paris Olympics, confirmed the risks involved.“In elite sport, it is almost non-negotiable that high-performing athletes choose supplements that are not only evidence-based but also third-party tested,” she told TOI.Athletics coaches, both former and current, who have followed India’s progress over the past few decades, recalled that Indian athletes have never undergone such intense testing before a major Games.“What the AIU has done on behalf of WADA is targeted testing of India’s top athletes who will be competing at the Asian Games. Across Bengaluru, Bhubaneswar and Patiala, officials have tested most athletes in the squad. This is the first time they have conducted such large-scale random testing of Indian athletes ahead of a major meet,” sources told TOI.“A few years ago, WADA attempted to test Indian athletes training in Potchefstroom, South Africa, but achieved limited success as many were unavailable. Athletes cannot be penalised for missing random tests, unlike those in the Registered Testing Pool (RTP), who are bound by the whereabouts clause,” they added.After testing athletes residing at the Kalinga Stadium complex in Bhubaneswar, officials also conducted checks on those training in Bengaluru at the Anju Bobby Sports Foundation and the SAI South Centre.India topped the AIU’s list of doping offenders in July this year with 162 names, ahead of Kenya (148) and Russia (60). The AIU also reclassified the Athletics Federation of India (AFI) from Category B to Category A.“Unfortunately, the quality of the domestic anti-doping programme is simply not proportionate to the doping risk,” AIU Chair David Howman had said.
Article Summary: The Athletics Integrity Unit (AIU) is conducting random checks on India’s elite athletes preparing for the Asian Games. Experts are concerned that the use of herbal supplements could result in Adverse Analytical Findings (AAF) when samples are tested for performance-enhancing substances abroad.

Article Title: 'A bit abnormal': After shock second-round exit at US Open, Auger-Aliassime reveals he 'was seeing spots'
Article Text:
Felix Auger-Aliassime, of Canada, serves the ball to Karen Khachanov, of Russia, during the second round of the U.S. Open tennis championships Thursday, Sept. 3, 2026, in New York. (AP Photo)

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Karen Khachanov knocked out third seed Felix Auger-Aliassime from the US Open on Thursday, winning 6-7(5), 6-3, 6-2, 6-2 to reach the third round.The Russian, ranked No. 50 in the world, came into the tournament after losing the opening match in all three of his US Open warm-up events. But he took advantage of an off-colour Auger-Aliassime, whose level dropped as the match went on at Louis Armstrong Stadium.After the match, Auger-Aliassime said he started feeling unwell during the contest and struggled to recover."After a set and a half, I just couldn't feel well and was dizzy and seeing spots and couldn't recover," he said, as quoted by BBC. "I thought maybe it would pass, but it didn't."I've never felt quite like that. I've had cramps before. I've felt tired towards the end of matches, but in a normal way."This was abnormal a little bit, and there were no signs in the last couple of days and no signs this morning, as well."The defeat made Auger-Aliassime the highest-ranked player to exit the men's singles draw so far in New York.Khachanov, who reached the US Open semi-finals in 2022, broke the Canadian's serve seven times during the match. He also saved seven of the nine break points he faced.The win is only Khachanov's second victory over a top-10 player at a Grand Slam and sends him into the third round in New York.The result meant Khachanov has now reached the third round of all four Grand Slam tournaments in a single ​calendar year for the first time.
Article Summary: Karen Khachanov knocked out third seed Felix Auger-Aliassime from the US Open. Russian, ranked No. 50 in the world, won 6-7(5), 6-3, 6-2,6-2 to reach the third round.

Article Title: Kidambi Srikanth pulls off stunning upset, Satwik-Chirag reach China Masters quarterfinals
Article Text:
Kidambi Srikanth

Former world No. 1 Kidambi Srikanth produced a stunning comeback to upset world No. 9 Victor Lai of Canada, while the men’s doubles pair of Satwiksairaj Rankireddy and Chirag Shetty battled a mid-match slump to reach the quarterfinals of the China Masters Super 750 badminton tournament in Shenzhen on Thursday.There was disappointment, however, for young Tanvi Sharma and the mixed doubles pair of Dhruv Kapila and Tanisha Crasto.Tanvi fought hard against Japan’s Tomoka Miyazaki but went down 17-21, 21-18, 16-21.Dhruv and Tanisha suffered an 18-21, 18-21 defeat to Liu Kuang Heng and Hsu Yin Hui of Chinese Taipei.Srikanth, the 2021 World Championships silver medallist, displayed remarkable fighting spirit to overcome World Championships bronze medallist Lai 21-18, 21-19.Later, he said: “I was only thinking about what I have been doing throughout the match and what I need to do going forward.”Srikanth added: “He has been playing well for the last 12-14 months. But I felt I’ll have my chances if I can play my best. I wasn’t thinking about how he has been playing. I was only thinking about how I should play.”Srikanth will next take on Hong Kong’s Lee Cheuk Yiu for a place in the semifinals.Meanwhile, Satwiksairaj and Chirag overcame a determined challenge from Frenchmen Christo Popov and Toma Junior Popov to register a 21-15, 22-24, 21-9 victory.They now face the Danish pair of Kim Astrup and Anders Skaarup Rasmussen in the quarterfinals.
Article Summary: Kidambi Srikanth produced a stunning comeback to upset world No. 9 Victor Lai of Canada. Satwiksairaj Rankireddy and Chirag Shetty battled a mid-match slump to reach the quarterfinals of the China Masters Super 750 badminton tournament.

Article Title: Treesa-Gayatri’s coach missing from list, WFI finally clears foreign coaches
Article Text:
India's Treesa Jolly and Gayatri Gopichand Pullela (ANI Photo)

New Delhi:

WFI finally relents on foreign coaches

Only seven grooms in equestrian

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

In squash, Willstrop will be foreign coach

Hockey without women’s masseuse

India’s latest women’s doubles hope, BWF World Championships bronze medallists Treesa Jolly and Gayatri Gopichand, will head to the Asian Games without their dedicated coach B Sumeeth Reddy, whose name does not figure in the official coaching and support staff list for badminton, while the Wrestling Federation of India (WFI) has finally agreed to send all three foreign coaches despite its initial reluctance, following a Sports Authority of India (SAI) rebuke.Reddy, a former Olympian who retired in March 2025, has specifically worked with Treesa and Gayatri since then, while also overseeing other women’s doubles players at the Pullela Gopichand Academy in Hyderabad. He was a constant presence in their coaching corner at international events and during the recent Worlds in New Delhi, sitting alongside Gopichand and guiding the pair through their matches.Treesa and Gayatri ended India’s 15-year wait for a women’s doubles medal at the Worlds since 2011, producing a string of impressive performances to claim bronze.Their Asian Games place had earlier come under scrutiny after sports authorities questioned their selection against the prescribed criteria, with Priya Konjengbam and Shruti Mishra emerging as alternatives. Badminton Association of India (BAI) defended the selection on rankings and recent performances.TOI contacted a senior federation official to ascertain whether Reddy’s name had originally been forwarded to the Indian Olympic Association (IOA) as an official women’s doubles coach.A call to a BAI official did not elicit a response.It has been learnt that Gopichand will carry the primary responsibility of guiding Treesa and Gayatri in Reddy’s absence. Tan Kim Her, who specifically works with Satwiksairaj Rankireddy and Chirag Shetty, could assist the women’s pair if schedules do not clash. South Korean Yong Sung Yoo, Lakshya Sen’s personal coach has received clearance. Twelve coaching and support personnel have been named for the 20-member badminton team.For wrestling’s 16-member squad, 14 coaching and support personnel have been listed, with all three foreign coaches now set to travel: Georgia’s Emzarios Bentinidis (men’s freestyle), Russia’s Gogi Koguashvili (greco-roman) and Japan’s Kosei Akaishi (women’s team). WFI had initially resisted sending them, preferring Indian coaches over them, but agreed after SAI questioned their omission.According to sources, the Equestrian Federation of India’s (EFI) ad-hoc committee had proposed 20 grooms for the eight-member equestrian team, but only seven have received clearance. The 12-member coaching and support staff list includes Nico Wienstroer, Katharina Asbeck, Kyra Anne Jonkers, Jill Van Osselt, Tabea Linhardt, Johanna Aini Katariina Pohjonen and Alyson Renee Roy as the seven grooms.SAI had also sought an explanation over the original proposal, with no groom named for dressage rider Jai Sud or eventing specialist Arjan Nagra.Former world No. 1 James Willstrop has been granted the SAI’s clearance to serve as India’s foreign squash coach receiving the nod for the same. The Englishman is expected to arrive in Chennai on Sept 17 before travelling with the team.The 40-member hockey squad has 14 support staff, and male masseur Arup Naskar is the sole masseur listed.
Article Summary: Treesa Jolly and Gayatri Gopichand will head to the Asian Games without their dedicated coach B Sumeeth Reddy. The Wrestling Federation of India (WFI) has finally agreed to send all three foreign coaches despite its initial reluctance. Former world No. 1 James Willstrop has been granted the SAI's clearance to serve as India’s foreign squash coach receiving the nod for the same.

Article Title: Neeraj Chopra’s replacement: Yashvir Singh drafted into India’s Asian Games javelin squad
Article Text:
India's Neeraj Chopra, right, and Yashvir Singh in a photograph after the men's javelin throw final at the Commonwealth Games 2026. (PTI Photo)

New Delhi:

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Know Yashvir

Glasgow Commonwealth Games bronze medallist javelin thrower Yashvir Singh has been drafted into India’s Asian Games athletics squad, replacing two-time Olympic champion Neeraj Chopra , who was ruled out for the season following an ankle ligament tear.Yashvir, who recently threw a personal best of 85.41m at the Commonwealth Games in Glasgow, will team up with the in-form Rohit Yadav (personal best 87.05m) to anchor India’s two-member men’s javelin campaign at Aichi-Nagoya.Meanwhile, former long jumper and Athletics Federation of India (AFI) senior vice-president Anju Bobby George will not travel as team leader, it’s been learnt. Though proposed by the AFI, her name was not cleared by the sports ministry adhering to its guidelines which say: IOA will ensure that any person, if he/she is holding elected position in EC of IOA, any NSF or any sports body, whose name has been included in the list of team officials, will be treated at no cost to the govt.The final athletics squad strength has been pruned to 77. Distance runner Abhishek Pal was dropped after testing positive for clomiphene. “It is not a case of returning dope positive, but as National Anti Doping Agency (NADA) investigates, we don’t want to take any risks,” said AFI planning committee chairman Lalit Bhanot. Additionally, 110m hurdler Tejas Shirse was ruled out due to foot stress fractures suffered during CWG.These two exclusions offset the latest addition of six athletes — Harita Bhadra (200m), Kiran Pahal (400m), Sindhushree G (pole vault), I Asha Ilango (triple jump), Sanya Yadav (discus), and Praveen Kumar (hammer throw) — who were cleared by the ministry after the Olympic Council of Asia (OCA) accepted IOA’s late request for their addition, bringing the count from 73 to 79 before Pal and Shirse’s omissions brought the contingent size down to 77.AFI is also seeking approval for Hangzhou double-medallist Avinash Sable to compete in the 5,000m alongside his confirmed 3,000m steeplechase event. However, Sable must first breach the AFI qualification mark of 13:39.18s at the Indian Athletics Series Finals here on Sept 10, where most Asian Games-bound athletes will compete.-- Born in Devsar, Haryana and raised in Jaipur, Raj.-- Shifted from basketball to javelin at age 13, initially practicing with bamboo javelins.-- Coached by his father Rai Singh, a former Indian Railways national champion.-- Broke Chopra’s U-20 Federation Cup record in 2021; joined the 80m club in 2022 (82.13m).-- Overcame major shoulder surgery in late 2023 that kept him out for nearly a year.-- Claimed bronze at Glasgow CWG with a final-throw personal best of 85.41m.-- Became only the third Indian male javelin medallist in CWG history after Kashinath Naik and Chopra.
Article Summary: Yashvir Singh replaces two-time Olympic champion Neeraj Chopra. Chopra ruled out for the season following an ankle ligament tear. Former long jumper Anju Bobby George will not travel as team leader. Distance runner Abhishek Pal dropped after testing positive for clomiphene.

Article Title: 'Encroacher' remark hangs over Yusuf Pathan as former India cricketer turned politician withdraws Gujarat high court appeal over Vadodara land dispute: Case explained
Article Text:
Yusuf Pathan (ANI Photo)

Pathan had challenged land allotment rejection

MP Yusuf Pathan during the Monsoon session of Parliament, in New Delhi. (PTI Photo)

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

VMC had asked Pathan to vacate plot

Yusuf Pathan campaigns with Rana Chatterjee (PTI Photo)

The Gujarat High Court on Monday dismissed as withdrawn an appeal filed by former India cricketer and Lok Sabha MP Yusuf Pathan against a single-judge order that had described him as an “encroacher” on a piece of government land in Vadodara.Pathan’s lawyer, Shalin Mehta, sought permission to withdraw the plea before a division bench comprising Chief Justice Sunita Agarwal and Justice DN Ray. The lawyer told the court that Pathan’s claim over the land was still being pursued under a state government policy.The division bench subsequently dismissed the appeal as withdrawn.The 43-year-old had approached the High Court challenging a single-judge order that upheld the Gujarat government’s decision to reject his request for allotment of the 978-square metre plot owned by the Vadodara Municipal Corporation (VMC).Pathan had claimed the land under a state policy applicable to international cricketers.During an earlier hearing, Pathan had told the court that he was pursuing his claim under a state government scheme and was given four weeks to pursue the matter. The High Court had also warned that he could face higher payment of damages if he took longer to vacate the plot.During Monday’s proceedings, Mehta said they were awaiting a response from the VMC but had not received one.“Because we are saying that there is a circular which allows international cricketers to be given a plot. I think I will withdraw because I haven’t heard anything from them (VMC). I have taken instructions from my client…if it is to happen, it will happen outside the court; otherwise it won’t happen," Mehta submitted.With the appeal withdrawn, Pathan’s attempt to challenge the earlier court order through the division bench has come to an end.The dispute dates back to 2024, when the Gujarat government rejected Pathan’s request for allotment of the plot. Despite the rejection, he continued to occupy the land.After Pathan was elected from the Baharampur Lok Sabha seat in West Bengal on a Trinamool Congress (TMC) ticket in 2024, the VMC issued him a notice asking him to vacate the land. Pathan refused and challenged the matter in court.The High Court had previously taken a strong view of his occupation of the plot. During a hearing on June 8, the court came down heavily on Pathan over the alleged “encroachment” and orally questioned how he could enter and occupy the land without completing the required formalities.The matter now moves outside the court as Pathan continues to pursue his claim under the state policy.
Article Summary: Gujarat High Court dismisses appeal filed by former India cricketer Yusuf Pathan. Pathan had challenged a single-judge order that had described him as an “encroacher’ on a piece of government land in Vadodara. The 43-year-old had approached the High Court challenging the decision.

Article Title: The long game: Inside MLB's big bet on India's baseball future
Article Text:

The broadcaster paradox

More than nine innings: Enter MLBX

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

A future where his job disappears

NEW DELHI: When Major League Baseball (MLB) opened its office in India in 2019, it wasn't the beginning of its journey in India. It was the culmination of a 15-year wait.For Ryo Takahashi, MLB's Director of International Business and the man leading its operations in India, the timing wasn't driven by a grand strategic moment or a blockbuster announcement. It was simply when years of conversations finally turned into an official commitment."People think MLB suddenly discovered India in 2019," Takahashi said in a free-wheeling chat with TimesofIndia.com. "The reality is we had been discussing India for almost 15 years before opening the office. There wasn't a magical reason why it happened in 2019. That's simply when we received the approvals and could make the commitment official," he said.Seven years later, MLB's ambitions in India still look very different from those of most global sports leagues. There are no plans for a professional franchise, no immediate push for a domestic league and no obsession with television ratings. Instead, the league is betting on a deceptively simple idea: if enough children pick up a baseball, everything else will eventually follow.India became MLB's sixth international office after Japan, Mexico, China, the UK and the Dominican Republic.But unlike those markets, baseball arrived with almost no cultural footprint here. That forced the league to begin by listening rather than selling."We don't believe we have all the answers," Takahashi says. "The NBA, La Liga, the Premier League -- they've all spent years understanding Indian fans. I have friends and colleagues across those organisations, and we've learnt as much from their mistakes as their successes," he added.Rather than copying another league's blueprint, MLB chose to build its own Indian version: one centred on schools, grassroots coaching and local storytelling. Since 2019, it has introduced the First Pitch programme in schools across Delhi, Mumbai and Bengaluru, launched the MLB Cup youth tournament and produced India-focused documentaries to make baseball feel more relatable.Ask Takahashi when India will produce its first Major League player, and he gently rejects the premise."People ask us when India will produce an MLB player. That's the wrong starting point," he says. "If one out of every hundred children who tries baseball decides to keep playing, that's already a victory. In a country of India's size, one per cent becomes a very big number."For MLB, participation is the primary currency, not finding elite talent."Our responsibility is to create opportunities. Whether that child eventually plays for an MLB club or simply falls in love with baseball, both outcomes help grow the sport," he reasoned.That thinking explains why MLB measures success through expanding coaching networks, more schools adopting baseball and the remarkable growth of the MLB Cup, which has evolved from just 12 teams in its inaugural edition into a nationwide youth competition involving thousands of participants.Conventional wisdom says cricket makes life impossible for another bat-and-ball sport. Takahashi argues the opposite."Cricket isn't our competitor. It might actually be our biggest advantage," he says. "Indian kids already grow up throwing, catching and hitting a ball. Those athletic foundations are already there," he explained.He has watched six-year-olds experience baseball for the first time and noticed how naturally many adapt."We don't have to teach them how to throw; we just have to show them a different game."MLB's objective isn't replacing cricket but borrowing from its ecosystem. Familiar movements reduce the learning curve, making baseball feel less foreign than many assume.Baseball's biggest obstacle in India isn't awareness alone. It's the clock.Most MLB games unfold in the early hours of the morning for Indian audiences, creating what Takahashi calls a classic chicken-and-egg problem.Even with broadcast partnerships in place with JioStar, he knows the league's target audience isn't awake."We want children to watch baseball, become curious and then play," he says. "But our games often happen at two or three in the morning in India.""An eight-year-old probably isn't holding the TV remote at that time. So maybe today's player becomes tomorrow's viewer. That's the journey we're trying to build."It's why MLB sees broadcasting as supporting grassroots rather than replacing it. A child introduced to baseball in school today may become the adult streaming the World Series a decade later.Perhaps Takahashi's most counterintuitive belief concerns infrastructure. While many emerging sports demand facilities first, MLB believes demand must precede concrete."People often say India needs baseball stadiums first," he says. "We actually think it works the other way around. First you create players, then you create demand, and eventually the infrastructure follows."He points to countless sporting cultures where children develop elite skills using improvised equipment and open spaces."Kids don't need a perfect baseball diamond to learn baseball. Skills come before stadiums."India already has cricket grounds, football fields and school playgrounds. For now, those are enough.That philosophy extends into MLB's biggest fan-facing initiative yet. Scheduled for October 24 in Mumbai, MLBX isn't designed as a traditional baseball tournament. It's a festival. Headed to the Mumbai Football Arena, Andheri Sports Complex, for MLBX are legends of the New York Yankees, Boston Red Sox, two-time defending champions Los Angeles Dodgers and Chicago Cubs."We asked ourselves: cricket evolved from Test matches to T20, football embraced futsal -- what’s baseball's version of that for India? MLBX is our answer," says Takahashi.The format features shorter games, compact fields, home-run contests, music performances and food inspired by classic American ballparks with Indian flavours. Baseball remains the centrepiece, but culture is the hook.The format or the tournament in itself is not new. MLBX is a mixed 3-on-3 baseball competition that combines power hitting, athletic defensive plays and fast-paced gameplay. The competition made its appearance during MLB All-Star Week in Philadelphia. The event has previously taken place at 15 US venues over the past three years, as well as internationally in London, Seoul and Mexico City."It's not just about games," Takahashi says. "It's home-run contests, music, food, culture and entertainment. We want someone to leave Mumbai thinking, 'That was fun... now let me find out more about baseball.'"He says the partnership with former India T20I captain and Mumbai Indians player Suryakumar Yadav has already generated a noticeable spike in enquiries, reinforcing MLB's belief that collaborating with cricket opens doors rather than closes them.Takahashi smiles when asked where he wants baseball in India to be by 2031. "My dream is to do such a good job that I make myself unemployed," he says almost with a grin.The answer is less about personal ambition than institutional success. He imagines an India with thousands more children playing baseball, a genuine national talent pathway, an active Indian national team and perhaps even baseball featuring if India hosts the 2036 Olympics."If, by 2031, baseball has become part of everyday sporting conversations in India, we've done our job," he says.For a league often associated with packed American ballparks and century-old rivalries, MLB's Indian strategy is strikingly patient. Its biggest victory may not be selling out a stadium. It may simply be convincing one child in a school playground to swap a cricket bat for a baseball bat.
Article Summary: Major League Baseball (MLB) opened its office in India in 2019. MLB's ambitions in India still look very different from those of most global sports leagues. There are no plans for a professional franchise, no immediate push for a domestic league. MLB is betting on a deceptively simple idea: if enough children pick up a baseball, everything else will eventually follow.

Article Title: 'We three sit together': India spinner reveals strategy after devastating spell against Pakistan in Women's Asia Cup
Article Text:
Shree Charani, Harmanpreet Kaur

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Young left-arm spinner Shree Charani said India’s spin bowlers plan their strategy together before matches and then focus on executing it on the field after Indian spinners helped bowl Pakistan out for 55 in their Women’s T20 Asia Cup clash.Charani returned figures of 3/7, while Prema Rawat took 3/9 and Deepti Sharma claimed 2/5 as India’s spinners took control of the match. Pakistan were bowled out for their lowest-ever T20I total of 55 before India chased down the target with 68 balls to spare and registered a seven-wicket win on Saturday.India had already secured a semifinal place from Group A before the match. They finished top of the group with six points after winning all three games.Charani, who dismissed Shawaal Zulfiqar, Gull Feroza and Ayesha Zafar, said the team’s spin bowlers discuss their plans before every match and then try to follow them on the field."In the meeting, we three sit together... Prema, me, Deepti di and Radha (Yadav) di and we discuss what to do (in the match). So, we just try to implement that here (on the field) whatever Deepti and Radha di say," said Charani.Pakistan had raced to 27 without loss, but Charani struck twice in the sixth over to leave them at 29/3.They could not recover after that and were eventually bowled out for 55.The 22-year-old is now one wicket away from completing 50 T20I wickets. She said her approach was to keep things simple and concentrate on getting the basics right."It's just about myself. Like I just want to focus on my things... I want to do my things correct," she said.After looking at the pitch and expecting it to help the spinners, Charani said she focused on bowling at the stumps and allowing the pitch to do the rest."I just tried to bowl on the stumps. By seeing the pitch, we know it may turn so I just focused on that."
Article Summary: India bowl Pakistan out for 55 in their Women's T20 Asia Cup clash. Shree Charani returns figures of 3/7, while Prema Rawat took 3/9 and Deepti Sharma claimed 2/5. India chased down the target with 68 balls to spare and registered a seven-wicket win.

Article Title: Indian spinner takes five-for in England, seals 213-run win in County Championship
Article Text:
Photo/screengrab

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Indian left-arm spinner Sai Kishore starred with the ball as Gloucestershire defeated Derbyshire by 213 runs in the County Championship Division Two match at the Seat Unique Stadium in Bristol.Sai Kishore returned figures of 5-20 from 18 overs as Derbyshire, chasing 319, were bowled out for 105 inside 39 overs during the final session of the match.Ed Middleton supported him with 2-17, while Ollie Price took 3-59, with Gloucestershire's spin attack claiming all 10 wickets in Derbyshire's second innings.The victory completed a turnaround for Gloucestershire, who had been reduced to 37-5 on the opening day of the match.Earlier, Gloucestershire declared their second innings at 359-5. Miles Hammond scored 118, while James Bracey remained unbeaten on 104. The pair added 165 runs for the fourth wicket.Bracey became the first Gloucestershire batter to score two centuries in the same first-class match since Alex Gidman achieved the feat at Archdeacon Meadow, Gloucester, in 2007.The win earned bottom-placed Gloucestershire 19 points and ended a run of six consecutive defeats.Their only two wins this season have both come against Derbyshire, who left Bristol with four points.Derbyshire needed early wickets when play resumed with Gloucestershire at 149-3, but they missed key chances in the field.Shoaib Bashir dropped Bracey off his own bowling when the batter was on five, while Matt Montgomery failed to hold a return catch to dismiss Hammond on 77.The missed opportunities proved costly as Hammond and Bracey took control. Bracey reached his second half-century of the match from 75 balls, while Hammond completed his third first-class century of the season and the eighth of his career from 182 deliveries.Derbyshire took the new ball and brought back seamers Ben Aitchison and Brett Randell, but Gloucestershire reached 268-3 by lunch.After helping Gloucestershire into a strong position, Hammond was dismissed when Montgomery caught him at mid-wicket off Martin Andersson. His innings combined defence and attack.Bracey then completed his fifth century of the season from 143 balls, hitting seven fours and two sixes before Gloucestershire declared at 359-5. He also became the first Gloucestershire wicketkeeper to score two centuries in a match since Harry Smith in 1919.Set 319 to win, Derbyshire's approach was focused on survival rather than chasing the target. Gloucestershire opened the bowling with spin from both ends and packed the field around the bat.Sai Kishore made an immediate impact after tea. He trapped Harry Came lbw and then bowled Matt Montgomery with the very next delivery.Soon after, Wayne Madsen was caught at second slip off Sai Kishore as Derbyshire slipped to 32-3.Mohammed Bin Naeem was then trapped lbw by Ollie Price after a delivery stayed low.Derbyshire's collapse continued as Sai Kishore bowled Aneurin Donald and Brooke Guest within three deliveries, completing his five-wicket haul inside eight overs.Middleton replaced Price from the Ashley Down Road End and had Ben Aitchison caught by Ollie Price at second slip with Derbyshire at 76-7.Martin Andersson, who top-scored with 35, was then caught at first slip after edging Middleton while trying to defend.Price wrapped up the innings by trapping Jack Morley lbw and then dismissing Brett Randell in front. He finished with match figures of 9-104 as Gloucestershire completed a 213-run win in front of home supporters.
Article Summary: Sai Kishore took 5-20 from 18 overs as Derbyshire were bowled out for 105. Ed Middleton supported him with 2-17, while Ollie Price took 3-59. Gloucestershire declared their second innings at 359-5. Miles Hammond scored 118 and James Bracey remained unbeaten on 104.

Article Title: ‘200, 300 mar de’: Vaibhav Sooryavanshi’s coach makes huge demand ahead of Duleep Trophy final
Article Text:
Vaibhav Sooryavanshi (PTI Photo)

Kolkata:

STOI

Main to chahta hun wo 200 mar de, 300 mar de, sab record tod de

On Teacher’s Day, the eve of the Duleep Trophy final, Manish Ojha has one particular wish — that his most famous ward, Vaibhav Sooryavanshi, produces a record-breaking knock when East Zone take on South Zone in the title clash starting Sunday. Vaibhav ’s childhood coach, who watched East Zone’s semifinal in Bengaluru, is in Chennai for Sunday’s title clash against South Zone, hoping the 15-year-old can make the most of a venue where he has already left his mark. Vaibhav scored 104 for India A against Australia A in a Youth Test here on Oct 1, two years ago, and Ojha believes that familiarity could work in his favour as he bids to strengthen his red-ball credentials.However, Vaibhav will not be the only player from Bihar and Jharkhand under the spotlight. East’s campaign has been powered by a strong contingent from the two states, with captain Ishan Kishan , Vaibhav, Anukul Roy and Mukesh Kumar regulars in the side, while Virat Singh and Kumar Kushagra add further depth. They are complemented by Bengal’s Mohammed Shami and Abhimanyu Easwaran, giving East a blend of youth and proven red-ball experience.The stakes are higher with the national selection panel, led by chief selector Ajit Agarkar, expected to watch the final. For Ishan and Vaibhav, in particular, the match offers a chance to underline their red-ball worth in front of the selectors and strengthen their cases for India’s Test setup.“Vaibhav has his own method and his own way of making runs. Ultimately, what matters is the performance and whether you are making runs for your team. He does that. His style of making runs is different,” Ojha toldfrom Chennai on Saturday.The coach is also impressed by the maturity Vaibhav is beginning to show despite his age and aggressive approach.“He is not even 16 yet, so give him time. Slowly, as he keeps playing, you can see the maturity coming into his game. According to the situation of the match, he is starting to change his game little by little,” Ojha said.“By the time he is 24, I feel he will still have another eight to 12 years of cricket ahead of him. You will expect a lot from him then, and I believe he will stand up to those expectations.”East’s return to the final after 14 years carries historical significance. Their last Duleep Trophy triumph came in the 2012-13 season, when they defeated Central Zone in the final in Chennai. A return to the city gives the current side an opportunity to recreate that piece of history.Former India and Jharkhand cricketer Shahbaz Nadeem believes East’s balance makes them strong contenders against South Zone.“Look at Shami, look at Ishan, look at Virat Singh and Anukul. There is a lot of experience as well as young blood. I think this mixture of youth and experience is a very good and, I would say, deadly combination,” Nadeem said.For Nadeem, reaching the final itself is a significant achievement for East after such a long wait.“It is always a premier tournament in India. If you are playing the final of such a tournament and representing a zonal team, there is nothing bigger than getting an opportunity to perform there. East Zone are reaching the final after many years, so I think it is very important for the boys,” he said.Nadeem also expects Anukul to play an important role in Chennai after a productive run in domestic cricket and with India A recently.“I think he will be quite useful on the Chennai wicket because he also bowls. His batting is also a plus point and his fielding is another plus point. This will be an important match for him to prove himself and give the selectors a statement that ‘I also belong at that level’,” he said.Meanwhile, for Ojha, Saturday’s Teacher’s Day has a special resonance. He is in Chennai watching a pupil he helped shape take another step towards the highest level.His wish for Sunday is simple. “(I wish him to score 200, 300 (in the game) and smash all the records,” Ojha says in jest and hopes Vaibhav turns his familiarity with the Chennai pitch into a big red-ball statement — and perhaps another record to remember.
Article Summary: East Zone take on South Zone in the Duleep Trophy final on Sunday. Vaibhav Sooryavanshi, 15, is the star player for East Zone. His childhood coach Manish Ojha is in Chennai to watch the final.

Article Title: Mohammed Shami hungry as ever: Ishan Kishan ahead of Duleep Trophy final
Article Text:
Mohammed Shami

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Chennai: Veteran India speedster Mohammed Shami maybe out of India reckoning for now, but he still refuses to give up. When East Zone play South Zone in the Duleep final at the MA Chidambaram Stadium here on Sunday, the 36-year-old will be appearing in his 100th First-Class match, with a prolific record of 382 wickets so far.East Zone skipper Ishan Kishan was effusive in his praise of the senior bowler on the eve of the title clash, stressing that age remains irrelevant when backed by exceptional work ethic and fierce determination."For Shami, age is just a number. If he is working hard, it doesn't matter. Having someone like him in our team gives us immense confidence. His approach towards the game, his intensity, and his energy this season have been very different from how I've seen him in the past," Kishan said after a practice session.Comparing this version of Shami to his sensational 24-wicket run at the 2023 ODI World Cup, Kishan stressed on the pacer's sheer appetite for a national comeback."It is 2026 now, three years since that World Cup. It is hard when you are not regularly playing for the Indian team to still summon that same motivation for domestic games...Who better than me can judge hunger right now? I see that hunger and drive in him, he wants to make that comeback and be part of the Indian squad again.You can see it in the way he helps me lead, constantly coming up with strategic options. You can instantly tell when a player is desperate to win you the match," the skipper added.Kishan also hailed Shami's tireless attitude during East Zone's semifinal victory over Central Zone, where the veteran ran in and picked five wickets in the game."He is a legend of the game. Looking at his effort in the semifinal, as a captain, it felt incredible when Shami came up and asked for extra overs to break partnerships. That willingness gives a skipper immense confidence. Plus, he finished with two boundaries in the last game, so he's practically an allrounder nowadays," Kishan quipped.South Zone captain Tilak Varma acknowledged the massive challenge awaiting his batting unit against Shami's probing spells with the red ball, but they are confident to face him."It will be great competition. We are up against a quality bowling attack led by Shami. Facing that calibre of bowling is why you love this sport," Tilak said.
Article Summary: Mohammed Shami will play in his 100th First-Class match on Sunday. East Zone skipper Ishan Kishan was effusive in his praise of the senior bowler. South Zone captain Tilak Varma acknowledged the massive challenge awaiting his batting unit.

Article Title: Women's Asia Cup: Another stroll in the park for India against Pakistan
Article Text:
Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Pakistan's women's team slumped to their lowest-ever T20I total as India cruised to a seven-wicket win in their 2026 Women's Asia Cup Group A clash at the Dubai International Cricket Stadium on Saturday night.Opting to bat first, Pakistan made a reasonable start, reaching 27 without loss in the fifth over through openers Muneeba Ali (13, 15b, 1x4) and Shawaal Zulfiqar (14, 14b, 3x4), both of whom benefited from dropped chances.However, India's spinners took control soon after, triggering a dramatic collapse. Pakistan lost six wickets for just eight runs in 28 balls to slide to 35 for six in the 10th over. Playing their 200th Women's T20I, Pakistan were bowled out for 55 in 18.1 overs, going below their previous lowest T20I total of 56 against New Zealand in Dubai in 2024. Their previous lowest total in the Asia Cup was 63.India's spinners made captain Harmanpreet Kaur's milestone match memorable, using skill, control and assistance from the slow pitch to stifle Pakistan. Left-arm spinner Shree Charani led the attack with three for seven in four overs, while leg-spinner Prema Rawat took three for nine. Experienced off-spinner Deepti Sharma finished with two for five in 3.1 overs.Charani dismissed Shawaal, who missed a sweep and was trapped lbw, Gul Feroza, who charged down the pitch and offered a leading edge to short third, and Ayesha Zafar, who was caught by Harmanpreet at mid-on. Charani is now India's highest wicket-taker in Women's T20Is in 2026, with 32 wickets in 18 innings.Part-time off-spinner Shafali Verma provided the first breakthrough, bowling Muneeba as the opener made room to cut a delivery that was too straight.India wicketkeeper Richa Ghosh also had a good outing, catching Nashra Sandhu off Rawat and pulling off a sharp stumping to dismiss No. 10 Tuba Hassan for nine.India were guilty of three dropped chances. Pratika Rawal put down Muneeba on six at cover-point off Kranti Goud in the third over, then dropped her again on nine at long-on off Shafali in the fifth. Rawal also dropped Pakistan captain Fatima Sana on nought off her own bowling in the ninth over.Pakistan, however, were unable to make India pay.Defending 55, Fatima Sana gave Pakistan their lone bright spell with a strong burst of seam bowling, taking three for 17 in three overs. She dismissed Shafali (12), Smriti Mandhana (9) and Pratika Rawal (4) to reduce India to 29 for three in four overs.Harmanpreet, playing her record 150th T20I as captain, steadied the chase with Deepti. Harmanpreet finished unbeaten on 18 off 18 balls, with one four and one six, while Deepti remained not out on 12 off 14 balls. Harmanpreet sealed the win with a six over long-on off Nashra Sandhu in the ninth over as India completed the chase with 68 balls to spare.India finished on top of the Group A table with three wins from three matches, while Pakistan must beat Hong Kong in their final group match on Monday to qualify for the semifinals.

NEW DELHI: Pakistan endured a dramatic batting collapse against India in their Women’s Asia Cup 2026 clash in Dubai on Saturday, crashing to their lowest-ever total in T20I cricket after being bowled out for just 55.After opting to bat first, Pakistan appeared to have an opportunity to put scoreboard pressure on India. Instead, their innings unravelled spectacularly as India’s bowlers turned the screw, with Pakistan losing six wickets for just eight runs after initially reaching 27 without loss.The 55 all out is now Pakistan’s lowest total in Women’s T20Is, surpassing their previous low of 56 against New Zealand in Dubai in 2024. It also becomes the fifth-lowest total conceded by India in a Women’s T20I.Only Pakistan’s two openers managed to cross double figures, with Muneeba Ali scoring 13 off 15 balls and Shawaal Zulfiqar making 14 from 14.The slide began after Muneeba survived a couple of early scares before Shafali Verma eventually cleaned her up. Sree Charani then struck twice in the final over of the powerplay, turning Pakistan’s promising start into a full-blown collapse.Pakistan went from 27/0 to 35/6, with India’s spinners repeatedly breaching a batting line-up that struggled to cope with the pressure.Charani finished with outstanding figures of 3/7, while Prema Rawat also claimed three wickets for just nine runs. Deepti Sharma chipped in with 2/5 and Shafali Verma took one wicket.The Indian attack's ruthlessness was reflected in Pakistan's inability to build even a single substantial partnership after the opening stand. With wickets tumbling at regular intervals, the innings was wrapped up for 55 in 18.1 overs.Charani credited a simple approach for her success."Just (trying) to bowl to my strength, and coaches are telling all bowlers, spinners especially, to bowl to strength and give more revs on the ball. [What deliveries are you working on?] Trying to get more consistency on my arm ball and be more accurate on the yorkers," she said at the break.The performance underlined why India had entered the contest with such confidence in their bowling attack. India had already secured a place in the semi-finals after winning their opening two matches against Thailand and Hong Kong, while Pakistan came into the game having beaten Thailand.The collapse came on a significant occasion for Pakistan, who were playing their 200th T20I. Instead of celebrating the landmark with a competitive total, they ended the innings with a record they would rather forget.Pakistan’s previous lowest all-out total in the format was 56 against New Zealand in Dubai in 2024. Their other lowest totals included 60 against England in Taunton in 2009, 63 against India in Guangzhou in 2012 and 65 against the West Indies in St Andrew’s in 2011.For India, meanwhile, the 55 all out added another dominant chapter to their recent record against Pakistan. India had won nine of their previous 10 T20I meetings, with their only defeat in that stretch coming in the 2022 Asia Cup.The contest also marked Harmanpreet Kaur’s record 150th match as a T20I captain, making her the first cricketer, male or female, to reach the landmark.
Article Summary: Pakistan bowled out for 55 in their Women's Asia Cup 2026 clash with India. Sree Charani took 3/7 and Prema Rawat claimed 3/9 for India. Pakistan lost six wickets for just eight runs after initially reaching 27 without loss.

Article Title: Rajasthan stuck in 2012, Manipur in 2023: How actively are states with CWG medals promoting sports?
Article Text:
Are sports bodies of Indian states promoting the game properly?

Poll Vote & Share your view What do you think is more important for grassroots sports promotion? Social media presence Local sports events Government funding 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion

NEW DELHI: Somewhere on a muddy school field in Haryana right now, a teenager is perhaps drilling the same throwing technique over and over, just as she had watched on television just days ago. Her sole aim is to pull off the one like Sharmila Dhankar, India's Commonwealth Games shot put gold medallist.Before the 2026 CWG campaign, she, like many of us, had almost certainly never heard the name. And it's not because Dhankar had not won anything before the Glasgow Games; she had, a gold medal in the Women's Shot Put F57 event at the 2026 Fazza International Para Athletics Championship, but because one of the primary institutions whose entire job was to carry that story back from the medal podium to villages and training grounds across the state has, for all practical purposes, gone quiet.That's the part of this story that rarely gets told. India walked away from Glasgow with 39 medals, and for a week, the athletes who won them were everywhere, garlanded at airports, seated beside ministers, their faces on the evening news. But medals don't build the next generation of athletes by themselves. Somebody has to keep telling their stories, long after the felicitation photo is filed away, to the kid training in a dusty school ground who needs proof that this path actually leads somewhere.We wanted to know which state sports departments are still doing their job of promoting the sports and their grassroots on their social media platforms, and which ones seem to have simply logged off. So we scrolled through the timelines ourselves. Here's what we found.No state produced more glory in Glasgow than Haryana. Eleven medallists, including seven gold, two silver, two bronze, spanning boxing, wrestling, athletics, and para sport, headlined by a Neeraj Chopra silver that will be replayed on sports channels for years.Alongside him were names most of India still had little knowledge of. The likes of Preeti Pawar, Jaismine Lamboria, Sakshi Chaudhary, Priya Ghanghas, Sachin Siwach, and Ankush Panghal, all of whom trained in government facilities, under government schemes, and who'd probably appreciate their own state department cheering as loudly for them as it does for its concert lineups.Because that's the thing. The Sports Department, Government of Haryana's X account has posted exactly once in all of 2026, and it's a flyer for the music acts playing at the Chief Minister's Cup.Facebook and Instagram follow a similar rhythm with a short cluster of posts around that February event, and then not much else.Eleven medals, and not one dedicated post to show for it. Somewhere in Rohtak or Bhiwani, a young pugilist training in Priya Ghanghas's discipline would probably just like a little proof that someone up top is paying attention.Manipur's page has an odd time-capsule quality to it. This is the state that gave India Mirabai Chanu, one of the country's most beloved Olympic medalists, and this Commonwealth Games alone produced four medalists from Manipur, Chanu's gold among them, alongside Rishikanta Singh, Bindyarani Devi, and Jadumani Singh.And yet the Department of Youth Affairs & Sports' X account hasn't posted since October 2023, a "Run for Unity" event, frozen well before any of this year's medals happened.Although the Facebook page has had a few sporadic posts here and there this year, its Instagram account has managed just two posts since January. It’s the kind of gap that makes you wonder if someone simply forgot the login details somewhere along the way.If there's one number in this whole exercise worth sitting with, it's this: the official Sports Department, Government of Rajasthan hasn't posted on Facebook since April 14, 2012.Fourteen years, through Arundhati Choudhary's Commonwealth gold and everything else that's happened in Rajasthan sport since.Its X account's last original post predates a retweet from March 2021, and there's no Instagram at all. A parallel handle, the Rajasthan State Sports Council, exists across all three platforms and is barely livelier.Somewhere behind Choudhary's medal is a genuinely good story, but it just hasn't found a home on the one page built to tell it.Gulveer Singh managed both a silver and a bronze for Uttar Pradesh this Games, a rare double that would make a great centrepiece for the state's sporting year. Instead, across two separate official handles on three platforms, Uttar Pradesh Sports has produced little beyond reposts, while its sister account, Sports Directorate, Govt of Uttar Pradesh, hasn't posted at all in 2026.Delhi Government, for its part, doesn't run a dedicated sports account at all on any of the popular social media platforms, so gold medalist Harsh Singh and bronze medalist Tejaswin Shankar, both representing India's capital, don't really have an institutional cheerleader online, their wins quietly absorbed into the general churn of city government updates. Both athletes are, in effect, doing their own promotional legwork.Set against all that quiet, Tamil Nadu feels like a different sport altogether. Its Sports Tamil Nadu handles post multiple times a day, celebrating not just its own three medalists, Praveen Chithravel, Selva Prabhu, Muthupandi Raja, but athletes from other states too, weaving in government scheme updates without it ever reading like bureaucracy.Every medallist got a dedicated post. Somewhere in Tamil Nadu, a kid training in long jump or wrestling doesn't have to wonder whether the sport leads anywhere. The state tells them, publicly, almost daily.Madhya Pradesh, Chhattisgarh, Karnataka's Facebook and Instagram pages, Assam, Bihar, and Tripura all follow a version of that same habit, active, consistent, generous with attention toward athletes nobody outside their district would otherwise know existed.Kerala doesn't run a separate sports handle on X but keeps its Facebook and Instagram genuinely lively, making sure Murali Sreeshankar and Mohammed Basil's silvers got their due.Andhra Pradesh mirrors that same rhythm across all three platforms.Not every state falls neatly into being inactive or staying proactive. Punjab's account managed just two posts on X all year, New Year's and Republic Day, though its Facebook and Instagram carry a bit more life around coaching and departmental meetings, even if athletes rarely get top billing.Uttarakhand was genuinely active last year before cooling off in 2026, leaning more toward government scheme announcements on Facebook, though its Instagram at least carried two posts around the Games.Maharashtra has dedicated posts up for both Sarvesh Kushare and Dilip Gavit, with Instagram staying fairly regular, enough effort to stay out of the quiet column.Karnataka's X account hasn't posted since March 2024, around an unrelated cultural-team event, even though its Facebook and Instagram have stayed warm and active toward its CWG medalists.It is worth asking why this actually matters, beyond good manners. Well, a state sports department's social media feed isn't just a courtesy board for congratulations; it's one of the cheapest, most direct tools available to build the next generation of athletes.A youngster in a small town is far more likely to pick up a javelin because they saw a state government post celebrating someone from their own district. Even when it comes to promoting any government policy, social media can be as effective.Visibility drives aspiration. There's a funding logic too. Sponsors, corporates, and even state finance departments allocate resources partly based on visible public interest, and a well-run social account is often the easiest evidence a sport has that interest.ALSO READ: Anahat Singh: What is in the name? A word from Guru Nanak's prayer, now India's squash sensation Silence, on the other hand, sends the message that grassroots sport isn't a priority worth the effort of a single post, even when the state has just produced a medallist on the world stage.It is worth it because sometimes, the first step towards building a sporting culture is simply showing people that their achievements are being seen.
Article Summary: India won 39 medals at the Commonwealth Games in Glasgow. Haryana produced 11 medallists, including seven gold, two silver, two bronze. But the state sports department has posted just once in all of 2026. What do you think is more important for grassroots sports promotion? Government funding or social media presence? Share your view.

NEW DELHI: Boxer Lovlina Borgohain's decision to object to a distorted Indian map during the Commonwealth Games earned special appreciation from Prime Minister Narendra Modi, who described the moment as one that would be remembered for a long time.Lovlina, who won silver in the women's 75kg category in Glasgow, was among India's medal winners who interacted with Modi at his residence on Sunday. The meeting, attended by Sports Minister Mansukh Mandaviya, Minister of State for Sports Raksha Khadse and Indian Olympic Association president PT Usha, saw athletes recount their experiences from the Games in an informal and emotional setting.In a little over 10-minute video of the interaction shared by the Prime Minister's Office on Monday, Modi brought up Lovlina's confrontation with a restaurant in Glasgow after she noticed a distorted Indian map.“Kya hua wo restaurant waale se jhagda kar rahi thi? (What happened, you were fighting with that restaurant guy?)” Modi asked.Lovlina laughed before explaining why she intervened.“We had such a good performance and it was the last day of the Games. It was a happy occasion sir, we were celebrating and I didn't like it when I saw the distorted map. I politely told them and they have made the changes also,” she explained.Modi applauded the boxer for noticing the issue despite being in the middle of celebrations after her medal-winning campaign.“To be able to recognise the significance of that map at a time when you were celebrating and the Games were over, I can tell you truthfully, that video was not ordinary. It will be remembered by people for a very long time,” he told the Tokyo Olympics bronze medallist.India finished fourth in Glasgow with 39 medals, including 13 golds, with boxing contributing seven gold medals.The interaction also provided an emotional window into Mirabai Chanu's journey to her gold medal in the women's 48kg category. The weightlifter produced a Games-record lift of 190kg, but her triumph came after four difficult years following her one-kilogram miss at the Paris Olympics. Modi asked Mirabai about the tears she shed on the podium and even fed her a laddu during their interaction.“Itne aansu tapak rahe the (So many tears were rolling down),” Modi remarked.Mirabai explained that the tears represented years of accumulated emotions.“I was very happy and emotional at that moment. I was crying because I missed a medal in the Paris Olympics by one kilogram. I have faced a lot in these last four years. I was battling injuries and some family problems too.“There were a lot of things. So, these four years were very tough for me. And when I stood on the podium, our flag went up and the anthem played, it was hard to stop myself,” she said.The meeting also had its lighter moments. Boxer Narender Berwal, who won silver in the +90kg category, recalled a funny exchange with a Pakistani boxer after beating him at the 2015 World Military Games.“During the 2015 World Military Games, I had a bout with a Pakistani boxer. I won it but when we were together in the medical room for treatment to our niggles, he said to me 'Bhaijan aapka naam Narender hai, aapke coach ka naam Narender hai, aapke Pradhan Mantri ka naam Narender hai, mujhe Narender naam se nafrat ho gayi hai.' (Brother, you, your coach and your PM are all named Narender. I hate this name now),” he recalled, drawing laughter from Modi.The Prime Minister also underlined the broader significance of the athletes' achievements, saying their medals were helping inspire a new generation.“I have been in this house for 12-13 years now and if there is one group that I have met regularly here, it is the athletes because of your efforts to win medals for India and your tradition of scaling new heights.“Far more than our push to promote sports in schools, it is your medals that inspire people,” Modi said.
Article Summary: Lovlina Borgohain won silver in the women's 75kg category in Glasgow. Prime Minister Narendra Modi described the moment as one that would be remembered for a long time. India finished fourth in Glasgow with 39 medals, including 13 golds, with boxing contributing seven gold medals.
